Article Title: An Indiana man used a painting to cover a hole in his wall; experts identified it as a Martin Johnson Heade, and Houston’s museum bought it for $1.25 million
Article Text:
A representative AI image of an antique painting concealing a damaged wall. (Image Credits: ChatGPT)

it

Two Magnolias on Blue Plush

From a cold email to a museum deal

Magnolias on Gold Velvet Cloth

catalogue raisonné

Image of Martin Johnson Heade-Magnolias on Gold Velvet Cloth. (Image Credits: Wikimedia Commons)

How an overlooked artist’s legacy resurfaced

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Finding a hidden work of art randomly seems to be the stuff of a treasure hunter’s dream. After all, a fortune does not always come with a certificate of authenticity or hang in a gallery under careful lighting. Sometimes, its value can go unnoticed until someone finally takes a closer look. One such story, almost out of a fantasy, happened when a board game prompted an Indiana homeowner to investigate a painting he had bought with a piece of furniture.The picture had been used to cover a hole in a wall. According to The New York Times, by May 1999, experts had identified it as a flower painting by Martin Johnson Heade, and the Museum of Fine Arts in Houston paid $1.25 million for it.The owner was a tool-and-die-company employee in his thirties and had paid next to nothing for it and the furniture. He likedbut remained clueless about its value. In January 1999, while playing Masterpiece, a board game, he noticed, a similar Heade.He went online, found that Kennedy Galleries handled Heade’s work, and emailed the gallery. He asked whether his painting was the work of that artist, then sent digital images of it.The gallery arranged for it to be authenticated and, once done, connected the discovery with the Houston museum. The seller was not identified in the report.The painting titleddates to about 1890. Theodore E. Stebbins Jr., author of the1975of Heade’s works, called it an important rediscovery and labelled it a fine example of the artist’s oeuvre. Stebbins, who was also curator of American paintings at the Museum of Fine Arts in Boston, added it to an updated edition of the catalogue.It was March 1999 when Martha J. Fleischman, president of Kennedy Galleries, told a decorative arts curator at the Museum of Fine Arts that she had made the find of her life, but could not yet say what it was. Emily Ballew Neff, the museum’s curator of American Art, contacted her and wanted to know when she could reveal it. After Fleischman identified the work, Neff immediately knew the museum wanted to acquire it.When the painting arrived for inspection, it remained in its original frame, almost in nearly perfect condition with the original glass protecting its surface. Subsequently, museum director Peter C. Marzio called an emergency meeting of the trustees. They approved the purchase in less than 90 minutes. One anonymous trustee provided most of the money, while two foundations supplied the rest. It was the museum’s first Heade and went on view on 2 June 1999, The New York Times reported. Other Heade flower paintings had also surfaced through sales. In May 1999, Christie’s sold Two Magnolias on Blue Plush for $882,500.Heade was born in Pennsylvania in 1819 and later became known for his landscapes, seascapes, hummingbirds, tropical scenes and flower arrangements. He settled in St. Augustine, Florida, in 1883 and painted many of his floral still lifes there. His magnolia works depict the different stages of blossoms at close range, and fewer than 20 were known, according to The New York Times.Christie’s American paintings expert Paul R. Provost offered one possible explanation for their rediscovery. Based on his assessment, people had bought Heade paintings while holidaying in Florida and taken them home. The works then passed down through families, whose members weren’t always cognisant of the artist’s work. Hence, some remained outside museums and eluded the attention of art specialists.Heade’s reputation had also fluctuated. According to Smithsonian magazine’s 2000 report, despite exhibiting frequently during a 60-year career, he was subjected to critical indifference. For a full four decades after he passed away, his work garnered little notice. An exhibition at New York’s Museum of Modern Art in 1944 helped revive interest. Art dealer Robert G. McIntyre saw Heade’s Thunder Storm on Narragansett Bay there and later recalled its artistic force and drama.The Smithsonian report also covered an exhibition organised by Stebbins to present the range of Heade’s work. It was displayed at the Museum of Fine Arts in Boston until 17 January 2000, before moving on to the National Gallery of Art in Washington and the Los Angeles County Museum of Art.
Article Summary: The Museum of Fine Arts in Houston paid $1.25 million for Martin Johnson Heade’s Two Magnolias on Blue Plush. Heade was born in Pennsylvania in 1819 and later became known for his landscapes, seascapes, hummingbirds, tropical scenes and flower arrangements.

Article Title: In 1967, an X-15 test flight killed Major Michael Adams; a remote California monument now marks the crash site of the experimental aircraft
Article Text:
The North American X-15. Image credits: Wikimedia Commons

Michael Adams reached the edge of space before the fatal crash

NASA’s investigation identified interacting causes

A Comprehensive Analysis of the X-15 Flight 3-65 Accident

A cutaway drawing of the North American X-15. Image credits: Wikimedia Commons

California memorial

marks the crash site

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

The X-15 programme continued until 1968

The North American X-15 helped researchers explore hypersonic flight and the conditions aircraft face near the edge of space. Its experimental flights advanced aerospace research, but one mission in 1967 ended in disaster. According to NASA.gov, U.S. Air Force Major Michael J. Adams lost his life when his aircraft broke apart during descent, leaving investigators to examine how technical problems, pilot workload and limited ground monitoring contributed to the accident.On November 15, 1967, Major Michael J. Adams took X-15 No. 3 on his seventh flight in the program. X-15 No. 3 was launched by an NB-52B carrier aircraft at an altitude of about 45,000 feet over Delamar Dry Lake, Nevada. In the flight, he achieved an altitude of 266,000 feet or 50.38 miles. This entitled him to receive the U.S. Air Force astronaut wings according to the altitude requirements. But soon enough, there were problems with the mission. As stated by NASA .gov, electrical disturbances early in the flight distracted Adams and made the aircraft control system less effective.During the wing rocking maneuver, the motions of the aircraft became too much and caused it to drift from its course.The X-15 then went into a spin at Mach 5 at around 230,000 feet. Adams recovered from the spin at 118,000 feet. But the aircraft then went into an inverted dive at Mach 4.7. There was a sustained oscillation with the MH-96 adaptive flight control system, which made the aircraft more difficult to control. The X-15 was flying at Mach 3.93 at around 65,000 feet. The aircraft experienced vertical loads exceeding 15 g and lateral loads of 8 g before breaking apart northeast of Johannesburg, California, 10 minutes and 35 seconds after launch.The accident investigation examined several factors rather than attributing the crash to one isolated failure. NASA’s 2014 assessment , revisited the accident and examined the relationship between aircraft malfunctions, pilot workload and the adaptive flight control system.Adams had to interpret cockpit data in connection with the electrical upset and a challenging hypersonic flight condition. The investigators also took into account the possibility that the pilot experienced spatial disorientation during the interpretation of the aircraft movement. The ground controller had their own set of difficulties. They did not have current heading information and could not interpret the movement of the aircraft properly. The original accident board had made certain recommendations, which included a telemetered heading device for ground controllers and the screening of X-15 pilots for vertigo.Adams’s astronaut wings were awarded posthumously because his flight went beyond 50 miles. His name was added to the Astronaut Memorial at the Kennedy Space Center in 1991. A second memorial to Adams was dedicated in 2004 near the crash site in California. The memorial sits in the Mojave Desert, northeast of Johannesburg, near where the experimental aircraft crashed. Its remote location follows from where the accident happened.Even after the loss of Adams and his aircraft, research with the X-15 continued. The November 15 flight was the last for X-15 No. 3 and the 191st flight of the program overall. In all, the X-15 fleet flew 199 times before the program ended on October 24, 1968. According to NASA’s historical records, the X-15 contributed to research on hypersonic flight and aircraft performance. Finally, the tragic accident of Adams was a clear demonstration of the significance of the flight control system, reliability, the precision of instrument measurements and efficient communication between pilots and crews on the ground.
Article Summary: The North American X-15 helped researchers explore hypersonic flight and the conditions aircraft face near the edge of space. Its experimental flights advanced aerospace research, but one mission in 1967 ended in disaster. U.S. Air Force Major Michael J. Adams lost his life when his aircraft broke apart during descent.

Article Title: Global droughts expose Texas dinosaur tracks, Yangtze statues, revealing climate change's surprising impact on archaeology
Article Text:
Dinosaur tracks in the Paluxy River bed at Dinosaur Valley State Park. Image credits: Wikimedia Commons

Texas drought reveals 113-million-year-old dinosaur footprints

Yangtze River drought exposes historic Buddhist statues

Research identifies

climate risks

to heritage sites

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

View of the Yangtze River near Chongqing, China. Image credits: Wikimedia Commons

Why does sudden exposure threaten historical discoveries?

Droughts can change landscapes in unexpected ways. As rivers shrink and reservoirs lose water, objects hidden beneath their surfaces can become visible. These discoveries give scientists opportunities to study the past, but they can also expose fragile remains to environmental damage. In August 2022, drought and heat revealed prehistoric dinosaur tracks in Texas and historic Buddhist statues from underneath the Yangtze River in China. These discoveries were noteworthy in terms of their significance in history. They also demonstrated how changes in the environment can have an effect on archaeological sites. While it is not possible to state that climate change is the reason for either discovery, it does increase the chances of extreme weather events.The dinosaur prints came into view in August 2022 as water levels dropped in the Paluxy River. According to the Texas Parks and Wildlife Department, the prints are about 113 million years old and normally sit underwater, often buried in sediment. According to the Texas Parks and Wildlife Department, the prints emerged when dinosaurs left their tracks on muddy tidal flats near the old sea, which eventually became hard and turned into limestone.Several prints belonged to Acrocanthosaurus, a big two-legged carnivorous dinosaur. Other prints came from Sauroposeidon, a huge long-necked, plant-eating dinosaur, according to the park. The prints gave insight into how dinosaurs lived and moved in ways that were not visible through skeletal fossils of dinosaurs. However, the discovery raised preservation concerns, since the prints are normally covered by water and sediment in the river. Once exposed, the limestone is more vulnerable to erosion.According to Reuters, a similar discovery was made in Chongqing, southwestern China, in August 2022 during a severe drought. Falling water levels in the Yangtze River exposed Foyeliang, a reef that is normally submerged, along with three Buddhist statues, according to Xinhua, China’s state news agency. The statues are believed to be around 600 years old and were initially identified as dating from the Ming and Qing dynasties. There were reports of a monk statue that was seated on a lotus pedestal. This discovery gave insight into the region's past religion and culture. However, such sudden exposure created problems regarding the preservation of submerged cultural sites. Changing water levels leave these stone carvings exposed to sunlight, temperature swings and erosion.The discoveries reflect a wider concern among heritage researchers. Climate change can intensify environmental conditions that threaten archaeological and palaeontological remains. A 2022 research article , “Climate Change and the Loss of Archaeological Sites and Landscapes: A Global Perspective,” discussed how climate change was creating new risks for archaeological sites and worsening existing vulnerabilities. The article identified increased rainfall, more extreme weather, rising sea levels and higher temperatures as pressures on archaeological landscapes. It also looked at how these changes affect different heritage sites and what archaeologists and conservation experts do to protect them. A separate 2025 study, “World Cultural Heritage sites are under climate stress and no emissions mitigation pathways can uniformly protect them,” published in Communications Earth & Environment , examined 938 UNESCO cultural heritage sites.The researchers found that about 80% of the studied sites were already experiencing climate stress and nearly 19% faced stress above the damage thresholds for both stone and wood. From the above-mentioned research, it can be understood that various types of building materials react differently to stress.Drought has allowed researchers to uncover artefacts that are normally underwater and out of reach. However, long exposure to such environmental conditions could contribute to degradation. The examples of the discoveries in Texas and the Yangtze River clearly indicate this issue. While decreasing water levels have led to the uncovering of historical artefacts, the same factors have made them susceptible to environmental conditions. Such cases do not prove climate change as the cause of these discoveries.
Article Summary: Texas drought reveals 113-million-year-old dinosaur footprints. Yangtze River drought exposes historic Buddhist statues. Climate change is not the cause of these discoveries, but it does increase the chances of extreme weather events. Changing water levels leave these stone carvings exposed to sunlight.

Article Title: A man searching a Massachusetts dumpster rescued 1,132 ancient Mexican artefacts; more than 40 Connecticut high school students then spent almost two years cataloguing them before their return to Mexi
Article Text:
Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

A routine house clearance in western Massachusetts nearly sent more than 1,100 pieces of Mexico's pre-Hispanic history to a landfill. Instead, a man's decision to investigate unusual objects in a dumpster set off an unlikely rescue operation involving an archaeologist and more than 40 high school students in Connecticut. According to a joint announcement by Mexico's Foreign Affairs and Culture ministries on August 17, 2026, all 1,132 objects were eventually returned to the Mexican Consulate in Boston after nearly two years of work to clean, classify, catalogue and document them.The discovery began around two-and-a-half years before the handover, when Matthew Pioggia was helping clear an old house in western Massachusetts. Among the discarded belongings in a dumpster, he noticed objects that appeared unusual. Knowing that his relative by marriage, Jeremy Pilver, was an archaeologist, Pioggia photographed some of the items and sent him the pictures, hoping he could identify them.Pilver, who teaches archaeology at Farmington High School in Connecticut, immediately recognised that the objects appeared to be genuine archaeological material. Although he could not initially determine their precise cultural origin or age, he realised they needed to be rescued before the dumpster was emptied.He urged Pioggia to retrieve as many as possible.In an interview with NPR, Pilver recalled that Pioggia climbed into the dumpster and spent about four hours digging through the discarded material. The objects were mixed with personal belongings, household debris and other waste. Pioggia eventually brought Pilver around 50 box tops filled with recovered material. The collection was in poor condition, with dust and debris covering the objects and their containers. Pilver also noticed evidence that mice and other animals had been around them.What followed was a painstaking project that turned a high school classroom into an archaeological workspace. Pilver enlisted his students to help examine and document the collection. Over nearly two years, more than 40 students participated in cleaning the surfaces of the objects, sorting and classifying them, creating a digital inventory and database, taking photographs, documenting individual pieces and preparing them for professional packing.Archaeological collections also carry information through their materials, designs, condition and associations. Recording those details systematically helps researchers study and compare objects, particularly when their original excavation context is not fully known. Pilver told NPR that the students worked through the collection using a shared spreadsheet and were deeply engaged in the project. He described the experience as an opportunity to show them the less glamorous but essential laboratory work behind archaeology.As the students worked through the boxes, they also uncovered an important clue to the collection's history. Pioggia had rescued paperwork along with the objects. According to Pilver, the documents indicated that the artefacts had been loaned from Mexico City's National Museum of Archaeology to a researcher connected with a US university around 55 years earlier. The paperwork provided a link to their Mexican origins, although it did not establish exactly how the collection eventually ended up in the Massachusetts house or why it was discarded.The inventory was subsequently assessed by specialists from Mexico's National Institute of Anthropology and History (INAH). Their examination identified the collection as pre-Hispanic archaeological material originating in southeastern Mexico. It included objects from different periods, meaning their precise dates and cultural associations still need further investigation. The documentation supplied by Pilver is expected to help specialists establish more details about the collection's provenance and chronology.The largest category consisted of 1,053 ceramic fragments, many of them believed to have been used for domestic purposes. The pieces included smoothed, moulded, painted and incised pottery. The collection also contained two complete spindle whorls, objects traditionally used in textile production, and 18 fragments of figurines. Other recovered material included nine flakes of obsidian, a volcanic glass commonly used by ancient communities to make tools, and 11 flint flakes. The inventory also recorded three wood fragments, three stone polishers, an incomplete slab of metamorphic rock, a fragment of another stone slab and 36 shark teeth associated with the archaeological material.The objects were not all elaborate or immediately recognisable as historical treasures. Some were fragments of everyday pottery, while others included small decorative pieces. In his NPR interview, Pilver described a small bird-shaped pendant that may have been worn on a necklace and an object he believed could have been an ear ornament. Their significance lay not only in their appearance but also in what they could reveal about the people and communities that made and used them.For Pilver, identifying the objects was only one part of the responsibility. He believed they belonged to the people and culture from which they originated and that returning them was the ethical course of action. He coordinated with the Mexican Consulate General in Boston, the Foreign Affairs Ministry and INAH to arrange the voluntary handover. The students also helped photograph, document and professionally pack the collection for its journey back.In August 2026, the consulate formally received all 1,132 objects during a handover ceremony. Mexico's government described the collection as one of the largest archaeological groups received by the Boston consulate in recent years. The return was coordinated by the consulate in collaboration with INAH, the Foreign Affairs Ministry and academic institutions in the New England region.Speaking to NPR, Pilver described the handover as an enormous relief after more than two years of work. He recalled how consulate staff came out to receive the boxes one by one, saying he felt as though he had taken his first deep breath in about two-and-a-half years. He was particularly moved by the response of Mexican officials, who recognised the significance of the gesture.The project also gave the students an unusual opportunity to put archaeological ethics into practice. Instead of learning about cultural heritage and repatriation only through textbooks and classroom discussions, they were directly involved in documenting and returning objects to their country of origin. Their contribution extended beyond identifying and sorting the pieces to creating a record that can support future research.Mexico's Culture Ministry said the documentation provided by Pilver would be used to establish further dating and provenance information, potentially allowing the objects to serve as a comparative collection for academic study. The return also forms part of the country's wider efforts to recover archaeological and historical material held abroad.
Article Summary: Matthew Pioggia was helping clear an old house in western Massachusetts. Among the discarded belongings in a dumpster, he noticed objects that appeared unusual. Knowing that his relative by marriage, Jeremy Pilver, was an archaeologist, he sent him the pictures, hoping he could identify them. Pilver enlisted his students to help examine and document the collection. Over nearly two years, more than 40 students participated in cleaning the surfaces of the objects.

Article Title: A New York co-op says a woman’s shower has leaked into the flat below, but she disputes it after about 10 inspections; the building is seeking nearly $170,000 in legal fees as a three-year dispute con
Article Text:
Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

A disagreement over a possible bathroom leak has turned into a costly legal battle between a New York homeowner and her co-operative apartment building, with the dispute now involving nearly $170,000 in legal fees. Guillermina Girardi, a resident of Manhattan’s Castle Village complex, maintains that her shower is not responsible for water damage reported in the apartment below. The building, however, insists that repairs are necessary. The case, reported by the New York Post and examined through decisions published by the New York State Unified Court System, has also raised questions about the authority of co-operative housing boards and the evidence required to establish responsibility for property damage. The dispute began in 2023, approximately six weeks after Girardi purchased her one-bedroom apartment for $660,000. Her downstairs neighbour, Ariane Zorgniotti, reported signs of moisture damage on her bathroom ceiling, including peeling and bubbling paint. Building management initially treated the problem as a relatively minor leak before later describing the situation as more serious.Castle Village eventually attributed the suspected leak to a possible defect in Girardi’s shower pan, the waterproof base beneath the shower floor.The building sought permission to enter her apartment and replace the shower installation, arguing that the responsibility for the repairs rested with the apartment owner under the co-operative’s rules. Girardi challenged the diagnosis, pointing to multiple inspections by New York City housing authorities that did not establish a leak originating from her apartment. According to the court records, inspections conducted by the city’s Department of Housing Preservation and Development in 2024 did not identify a cracked shower pan or confirm a leak in the downstairs bathroom. One violation was issued over peeling plaster and paint.The legal proceedings have produced different assessments of the available evidence. In March 2025, a New York Supreme Court judge found that the building had not provided sufficient evidence at that stage to establish the source of the alleged leak. The judge modified an earlier order, removing the requirement that Girardi allow immediate repair work while retaining the building’s right to inspect her bathroom.In June 2025, the same court declined to grant summary judgment to either side, finding that questions about whether a leak existed remained unresolved. The judge noted that the housing department’s inspection reports supported Girardi’s position, while the building had submitted statements from its staff and the downstairs resident, along with photographs of the reported damage.However, the legal position shifted in March 2026. New York’s Appellate Division, First Department, overturned the lower court’s decision and ruled in favour of Castle Village. The appellate court found that the building had presented sufficient initial evidence of a leak through photographs and sworn statements from its assistant superintendent and the downstairs resident. It directed Girardi to provide access for repairs at her expense under the terms of her proprietary lease. The court also rejected her argument that the building had deliberately singled her out for unfair treatment.The proposed work would involve removing her existing shower and replacing parts of the bathroom with standard building materials. The original estimate was approximately $9,200, although Girardi believes the actual cost could reach $40,000, particularly because the renovation would involve replacing the existing Carrara marble tiles.The conflict has also been complicated by an earlier disagreement over a building-wide gas-pipe replacement project. Girardi had objected to the proposed placement of a horizontal pipe across her kitchen ceiling, arguing that it would interfere with plans to create a private home office. The building subsequently took legal action to obtain access for the installation, and she eventually complied with the arrangement.Meanwhile, the financial consequences of the ongoing dispute have continued to grow. Castle Village is now seeking nearly $170,000 from Girardi in legal fees, adding another substantial expense to a disagreement that began with reports of water damage. The latest development came when a building contractor arrived at Girardi’s apartment intending to carry out the proposed bathroom work. She sought the contractor’s plumbing licence details and the necessary permit from the city’s Department of Buildings, but the information was not provided, according to the recorded interaction described in the New York Post report.Despite the appellate ruling, the disagreement over the proposed work, its cost and the legal fees has continued, turning what initially appeared to be a routine maintenance issue into a prolonged dispute between a homeowner and her co-operative building.
Article Summary: Guillermina Girardi, a resident of Manhattan’s Castle Village complex, maintains that her shower is not responsible for water damage reported in the apartment below. The building, however, insists that repairs are necessary. Castle Village is now seeking nearly $170,000 in legal fees.

Article Title: Endangered colourful San Francisco garter snakes released into the wild for the first time as 62 zoo-born youngsters begin life in California’s San Mateo County
Article Text:
Image: San Francisco Zoo and Gardens

Biologists see the first release as a step toward healthy populations that can sustain themselves

Image: San Francisco Zoo

Researchers estimate only a few thousand harmless, brightly coloured snakes remain in the wild

Genetic testing at the zoo decided where each head-started snake would be released

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Another generation of more than 130 snakes born at the zoo this year is waiting for release in 2027

Endangered San Francisco garter snakes have been released into the wild for the first time, a milestone for conservation in California. Sixty-two young snakes born at the San Francisco Zoo were set free at carefully chosen sites across San Mateo County, one of only two California counties where the species lives naturally, earlier this autumn. The reptile has featured on the United States endangered species list since its first edition in 1967, which makes this captive-bred release a significant turning point for the species. Wildlife managers hope the achievement clears the way for further releases of the same kind. The zoo said the release marks a major milestone in a decades-long effort to bring the species back from the brink of extinction.According to Popular Science, the successful rewilding of dozens of the endangered snakes is a huge moment for population rehabilitation efforts. Karine Tokatlian, a biologist at the Midpeninsula Regional Open Space District, said in a statement that the snakes’ return represents years of research, collaboration, habitat restoration and careful conservation work. She described the first release as an important step toward healthy, resilient populations that can sustain themselves over the long term. The San Francisco Zoo said the project brought together multiple agencies and organisations, combining scientific research, habitat protection and restoration with hands-on animal care to support the species’ recovery.The species has endured nearly six decades of droughts, invasive species, disease, low genetic diversity and poaching. The snake is slender but can grow anywhere from 18 to 55 inches long, roughly 46 to 140 centimetres. Its eyes are larger than those of most garter snakes, which allows it to stay active during daylight hours. With no fangs and only mildly toxic saliva, it is essentially harmless to humans, although its bites are fatal to prey such as smaller reptiles and rodents. The San Francisco Zoo said only a couple thousand individuals are estimated to remain in the wild. The species is found only in San Mateo County and a small portion of Santa Cruz County, and nowhere else on Earth.Head-starting is the process of rearing young animals in captivity before releasing them, which protects creatures during the most vulnerable stage of their lives. For these snakes it began in 2025, when conservationists collected several pregnant females from a healthy preserve in California’s Midpeninsula. Researchers released the adults back into their habitat after they gave birth and kept the infants at the San Francisco Zoo. After testing each snake’s genetics, conservationists placed about one-third in the same area as their mothers. The other two-thirds went to sites that particularly needed a bigger genetic pool for breeding. The zoo said the young snakes were raised until they reached a size better able to withstand threats such as predation and competition for prey.Release locations have not been disclosed to protect the snakes from illegal collection, vehicle mortality and disease.Biologists continue to monitor the first head-started generation, and the next batch is still being raised at the zoo. More than 130 additional San Francisco garter snake babies were born there in 2026 and are being prepared for another round of releases planned for 2027. Post-release monitoring will help researchers determine how effectively the two rounds of releases improve populations at their sites and what lessons can be applied to future head-starting efforts. Ariel Starr, a wildlife ecologist at the same district, added that the species’ critical status is not unique. She said the project’s success and research should hopefully inform the recovery of many other imperilled reptile species.
Article Summary: Sixty-two young snakes born at the San Francisco Zoo were set free at carefully chosen sites across San Mateo County earlier this autumn. The reptile has featured on the United States endangered species list since its first edition in 1967. Biologists see the first release as a step toward healthy populations that can sustain themselves.

Article Title: 24 militants, four soldiers killed in separate clashes in Pakistan's Balochistan and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa
Article Text:
(Photo credit: IANS)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

At least 24 militants and four Pakistani soldiers, including an army officer, were killed in separate encounters between security forces and militants in Balochistan and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa provinces, the Pakistan Army said on Saturday, PTI reported.The army said security forces had carried out multiple intelligence-based operations (IBOs) in Balochistan since Friday, targeting militant hideouts in the areas of Kolpur, Kardagap and Nushki.During an operation in Kolpur on the intervening night of Friday and Saturday, troops killed eight militants, including a suicide bomber, and recovered a large cache of weapons and ammunition, the military said.The army said the militants used armed quadcopters to target military vehicles on patrol. The attack killed Major Omer Minhas Nasir and Havildar Muhammad Adnan Khan.The Pakistani government last year designated terrorist groups operating in Balochistan as 'Fitna al Hindustan'. Islamabad has alleged that these outfits carry out terrorist activities at India's behest, but has not provided evidence to support the claim.In June, India criticised Pakistan at the United Nations over the use of the term, calling it "officially sponsored misinformation and disinformation dressed in religious terminology."Separately, security forces conducted operations against militant hideouts in Mir Ali, Datta Khel and surrounding areas of North Waziristan district in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.According to the Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR), the military's media wing, 16 militants were killed in the engagements. Twelve were killed in an operation in Ali Khel, while two each were killed in Mir Ali and Datta Khel.Two soldiers, Havildar Asmat Ali and Naik Aftab Ali, were killed during the operations. The ISPR said both soldiers fought bravely and laid down their lives in the line of duty. It added that the operations had dealt a major blow to the militant network.Weapons and ammunition were recovered from the slain militants, who, according to the military, were involved in several terrorist activities, including the killing of civilians.Pakistan's federal government uses the term 'Fitna al-Khawarij' for militants belonging to the banned Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP).
Article Summary: At least 24 militants and four Pakistani soldiers killed in Balochistan and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa provinces. Security forces carried out multiple intelligence- based operations (IBOs) since Friday, targeting militant hideouts in the areas of Kolpur, Kardagap and Nushki. During an operation in Kolpur on the intervening night of Friday and Saturday, troops killed eight militants.

Article Title: Suicide car bombing at security checkpoint in Pakistan kills 5, injures 13

At least 5 people have been reported dead and 13 injured after a car bombing at a security checkpoint in Pakistan’s Balochistan province, a security official reported on Friday.The attack took place on Thursday evening in the Kanda Wa area of Mastung district, along the N-25 national highway. The vehicle struck a Frontier Corps (FC) checkpoint, according to a security official quoted by PTI.The three militants killed in the attack included the bomber, while two civilians also died. The injured included FC personnel, the official said. However, Dawn, quoting Balochistan police, reported that at least 16 people were injured, including three members of the border forces.The banned Baloch Liberation Army (BLA) claimed responsibility for the bombing, identifying the suicide attacker as Osama Shahwani and saying he had joined the organisation in 2022.A security official, however, said Shahwani's name had appeared in a missing-persons case in 2024. The official alleged that the incident pointed to the BLA's recruitment of young Baloch men and its attempts to mislead authorities about their whereabouts.The injured were shifted to nearby hospitals for treatment. Security agencies are investigating the attack and the circumstances surrounding the bomber's links to the insurgent group.
Article Summary: At least 5 people have been reported dead and 13 injured after a car bombing at a security checkpoint in Pakistan’s Balochistan province. The banned Baloch Liberation Army (BLA) claimed responsibility for the bombing. The attack took place on Thursday evening in the Kanda Wa area of Mastung district.

Article Title: Pakistani teen mauled to death by tigress released from cage for TikTok video shoot
Article Text:
Pakistani teenager mauled to death after tigress freed for TikTok video in Lahore (Image source: X)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

A 19-year-old Pakistani teenager was mauled to death by a tigress after it was let out of its cage for a TikTok video shoot.The victim, identified as Talha, was working at a private breeding facility in Kahna, Lahore district, when the animal attacked him. He was rushed to a private hospital but died while undergoing treatment on Wednesday, according to local reports.Police identified the arrested farm owner as Fayyaz and the TikToker as Noman. Investigators allege that the influencer had visited the property to film a video and asked for the animal to be released from its enclosure. The animal subsequently lost control and attacked the worker, police said.The incident also triggered an investigation into an alleged attempt to conceal the circumstances of the death. Police said efforts were made to portray the attack as an incident involving a dog rather than a big cat. The animal has since been handed over to wildlife authorities.Authorities are examining whether the farm had the necessary permits to keep the animal and whether adequate safety measures were in place at the facility. A case has been registered and investigations into possible negligence are under way.In a statement, Lahore Police said that the pursuit of social media content could not come at the cost of human life. It said all aspects of the alleged negligence and the attempt to conceal the attack would be investigated.There has been some confusion in initial media reports over whether the animal was a tiger or a lion. Lahore Police's statement described it as a tigress.
Article Summary: The victim, identified as Talha, was working at a private breeding facility in Kahna, Lahore district, when the animal attacked him. Investigators allege that the influencer had visited the property to film a video and asked for the animal to be released from its enclosure.

Article Title: Imran Khan-Asim Munir deal? Sisters' release from jail, hospital visit spark buzz in Pakistan
Article Text:
Release of Imran Khan's two sisters and his hospital visit fuel speculation of a possible political understanding with Pakistan's military establishment

PTI ready to make peace?

Nawaz Sharif , Benazir Bhutto precedent

Why a deal may not be straightforward

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Is Pakistan witnessing the first signs of a possible thaw between jailed former prime minister Imran Khan and the country's powerful military establishment? The release of two of his sisters and his recent hospital visit for eye treatment have come amid speculation that a political settlement involving Army Chief Field Marshal Asim Munir has taken place.His sisters, Uzma Khan and Noreen Niazi were released on Thursday from Lahore's Kot Lakhpat Jail after the Punjab government withdrew their extended detention orders. The two had spent 53 days in custody after being detained ahead of a Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) protest march. Their sister Aleema Khan remains behind bars.The release came a day after Imran Khan was taken from Adiala Jail to Islamabad's Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences for an eye examination and treatment. Doctors administered an injection for an issue affecting his right eye, besides treating his blood pressure. He was discharged in the early hours of Thursday and returned to prison.The developments have coincided with renewed speculation about a possible deal involving Khan and the military establishment. Pakistan interior minister Mohsin Naqvi, however, dismissed reports of any behind-the-scenes arrangement on Thursday, saying Khan and his family would receive whatever relief the courts granted them.The possibility of a rapprochement is not entirely new. In August, one of Imran Khan's closest aides, PTI spokesperson Zulfikar Bukhari, had told Reuters that the former prime minister would not confront the military if released."If Imran Khan was released tomorrow, hypothetically, he wouldn't do anything that would effectively damage the country," Bukhari had said, describing him as "magnanimous".He had also suggested that Munir could take the initiative to ease tensions, saying the army chief could extend a "healing hand" to the country."That doesn't mean you go loggerheads with the establishment, with the military leader," Bukhari said, adding that personal grievances could be set aside in the national interest.The remarks marked a notable shift in the PTI's public rhetoric after years of confrontation with the military establishment following Khan's ouster in a no-confidence vote in 2022.Bukhari, however, had mentioned that there were no talks between the PTI and the military. He also acknowledged that it was unclear whether Khan himself shared the willingness to reconcile being expressed by party leaders outside prison.The latest speculation has also been fuelled by opposition leader Mahmood Khan Achakzai's claim in October that Khan could be facing pressure to accept an arrangement similar to those involving former prime ministers Nawaz Sharif and Benazir Bhutto.Sharif left Pakistan in 2000 after being ousted and imprisoned following the military coup led by General Pervez Musharraf. Bhutto spent years abroad in self-imposed exile after her government was dismissed in 1996.Achakzai alleged that the ruling Pakistan Muslim League-Nawaz and Pakistan Peoples Party were part of a political arrangement that could pave the way for a similar outcome in Khan's case. However, he did not establish that any such agreement had been reached.An exile arrangement could potentially offer a way out of the prolonged confrontation, but there is no confirmation that Khan has agreed to leave Pakistan or that negotiations with Munir are under way.Imran Khan's relationship with the military establishment deteriorated after disagreements over key appointments and foreign policy. He has accused the military leadership, including Munir, of orchestrating his removal. The military denies interfering in politics.Despite being in prison since August 2023, Khan remains the central figure in Pakistan's political confrontation. His party continues to demand his release, access to family members and lawyers, and relief in the cases against him.The PTI's position also raises a crucial question: can its leadership outside prison negotiate or signal a compromise without Khan's explicit approval? Bukhari's August remarks came with the caveat that the former prime minister's own thinking might be different.For now, the signals remain contradictory. Two members of Khan's family have been released, he has received medical treatment, and a senior PTI aide has previously spoken of reconciliation. But the government has denied any political bargain, and there is no evidence of direct negotiations with Munir.Whether the latest developments represent isolated legal and medical decisions or the beginning of a fresh political opening remains the question.
Article Summary: Imran Khan's two sisters were released from jail on Thursday after 53 days in custody. He was also taken to a hospital for an eye examination and treatment. The developments have fuelled speculation about a possible deal involving Khan and the military establishment. Pakistan interior minister dismissed reports of any behind-the-scenes arrangement on Thursday.

Article Title: 74 militants killed in Pakistan security operations along Afghan border in 10 days
Article Text:
43 militants killed in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa raids, 31 in Balochistan operations: Pakistan

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Pakistani security forces have killed 74 militants in a series of raids and operations in the country's northwest and southwest regions bordering Afghanistan over the past 10 days, the Associated Press cited military officials Friday.The raids were conducted in Mir Ali and Orakzai districts of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province, where troops killed 43 militants and recovered weapons, ammunition and explosive devices, the military said in a statement.Separately, security forces killed 31 militants in multiple operations in Balochistan province since November 3, the military said. The province has been witnessing a bloody insurgency led by the rebel Baloch Liberation Army (BLA).Kabul has denied accusations of providing support to militant groups operating against Pakistan.The Pakistani Taliban are a separate group from, but allied with, Afghanistan's Taliban, who returned to power in Kabul in 2021. Several TTP leaders and fighters are believed to be operating from sanctuaries across the Afghan border, a longstanding source of tension between Islamabad and Kabul.
Article Summary: Pakistani security forces have killed 74 militants in a series of raids and operations in the country's northwest and southwest regions bordering Afghanistan. The raids were conducted in Mir Ali and Orakzai districts of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province. Separately, security forces killed 31 militants in multiple operations in Balochistan province since November 3.

Article Title: BLA claims 18 killed in suicide vehicle attack on Pakistan Army camp in Balochistan
Article Text:
Baloch Liberation Army claims responsibility for a suicide vehicle attack on a Pakistani Army camp in Balochistan, claiming 18 personnel were killed

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Multiple casualties were reported in a VBIED attack at Pak army’s main camp in Mastung, Balochistan Thursday. The Baloch Liberation Army (BLA) took responsibility for the attack, claiming to have eliminated 18 personnel.According to BLA, its Fidayeen attack, the Majeed Brigade, carried out an operation in the Kanak area of Mastung, targeting a Pakistani military camp with a suicide vehicle-borne improvised explosive device followed by an assault by its armed fighters who entered the premises and targeted military personnel.The attack unfolded while a meeting of senior Pak Army personnel including colonel rank officials was underway when the mini-truck laden with explosives rammed into the main gate of the camp.The area has been on the boil since Wednesday. According to pro-BLA accounts on Telegram, Pak security forces were carrying out “operation Radd-ul-Fitna”, aimed at destroying tunnels allegedly made by Baloch rebels, on Wednesday and Thursday in the area.They claimed to have destroyed seven tunnels and seized arms, ammunition and explosives. In Musakhel, unidentified set ablaze construction machinery and a separate explosion destroyed a bridge in Mastung.On Wednesday, 13 Pakistani police personnel including a Deputy Superintendent of Police were killed after fighters from the rebel group Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) launched a major attack targeting mobile police units in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.
Article Summary: The Baloch Liberation Army (BLA) took responsibility for the attack, claiming to have eliminated 18 personnel. The attack unfolded while a meeting of senior Pak Army personnel including colonel rank officials was underway when the mini-truck laden with explosives rammed into the main gate of the camp.

Article Title: 'Some good news': Two sisters of ex-Pak PM Imran Khan released from jail; elder sister, wife remain behind bars
Article Text:
Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Two sisters of Pakistan's incarcerated former Prime Minister Imran Khan were released from a Lahore jail on Thursday after the Punjab government revoked their detention orders, leaders of his Pakistan Tehreek-i-Insaf (PTI) party said.However, his elder sister and wife remain behind bars."Finally, some good news. Two of former PM Imran Khan's sisters, Dr Uzma Khan and Noreen Niazi, have been released from Kot Lakhpat Jail following the withdrawal of their detention orders," PTI senior leader and former federal minister Moonis Elahi said in a statement."Hopefully, Aleema sahiba and Bushra Bibi, will also be released soon," he added, referring to the cricketer-turned-politician's elder sister and wife, respectively.Meanwhile, another senior PTI leader, Zulfi Bokhari, asserted that the release of Imran Khan's two sisters would not "erase the suffering" endured by his family."The release of two sisters does not end the injustice or erase the suffering inflicted on Imran Khan’s family. The demand is clear -- no selective relief, no intimidation, and no further persecution," Bokhari told party supporters.Imran Khan's sisters were detained in September under a public safety law to prevent them from mobilising support for a nationwide protest demanding his release.Bushra Bibi was arrested in January 2025 in a separate case in which the couple were sentenced.The 74-year-old PTI founder has been in prison since 2023 and faces more than 100 cases, including corruption charges and allegations of inciting violence.On Wednesday, PTI lawyers met Imran Khan at Rawalpindi's Adiala Jail to discuss his ongoing court cases, a day after the Islamabad high court directed authorities to facilitate the meeting.The lawyers spent four hours at the prison before leaving without speaking to the media.According to PTI lawyer Latif Khosa, who was part of the delegation, Imran Khan was experiencing problems with his blood pressure and eyesight.
Article Summary: Two sisters of Pakistan's incarcerated former PM Imran Khan were released from a Lahore jail on Thursday. The Punjab government revoked their detention orders, leaders of his Pakistan Tehreek-i-Insaf (PTI) party said. But his elder sister and wife remain behind bars.

Article Title: Pakistan announces schedule for Guru Nanak’s 557th birth anniversary celebrations despite Attari-Wagah closure
Article Text:
Pakistan has maintained that the Kartarpur Corridor remains open from its side (Photo: PTI).

AMRITSAR: Despite the continued closure of the Attari-Wagah international land border following Operation Sindoor, the Pakistan government has announced a programme for the 557th birth anniversary celebrations of Guru Nanak Dev, expecting between 2,300 and 2,700 Sikh pilgrims from India for the November 24 event at Nankana Sahib.Pakistan has also maintained that the Kartarpur Corridor remains open from its side, although pilgrim movement through it continues to be suspended by India.According to Pak media reports, the programme was finalised at a meeting of the Pakistan Sikh Gurdwara Parbandhak Committee (PSGPC), chaired by its president and Punjab provincial minister for minority affairs and human rights, Ramesh Singh Arora, to review arrangements for the celebrations.As per the schedule, Indian Sikh pilgrims are expected to arrive in Pakistan through the Attari international border on November 22. The main ceremony will be held on November 24 at Gurdwara Janam Asthan, Nankana Sahib, the birthplace of Guru Nanak Dev. The pilgrims are scheduled to return on December 1.Reacting to Pakistan’s announcement, Sikh scholar Jagdeep Singh said the proposed pilgrimage programme assumes significance amid strained India-Pakistan ties and the continued closure of the Attari-Wagah border after Operation Sindoor.“Keeping the border open would serve the interests of both countries and, above all, make it easier for devotees to visit their historic religious shrines,” said Jagdeep.Interestingly, while Pakistan maintains that the Kartarpur corridor is operational on its side and has expressed readiness to facilitate Sikh devotees, India has suspended pilgrim movement through it since May 2025.In a statement, Arora said Pakistani diplomatic missions had been instructed to facilitate visa issuance for Sikh pilgrims. He also urged India to allow the Sikh sangat to visit its historic shrines.According to reports, the arrangements reviewed at the meeting include air-conditioned buses, accommodation, langar, medical facilities, mineral water and currency exchange services. A Rescue 1122 ambulance will accompany every convoy of 20 buses to meet medical emergencies.
Article Summary: Pakistan has announced a programme for the 557th birth anniversary celebrations of Guru Nanak Dev. It is expecting between 2,300 and 2,700 Sikh pilgrims from India for the November 24 event at Nankana Sahib. Pakistan has also maintained that the Kartarpur Corridor remains open from its side.

Article Title: 'Two eight-year-olds or four four-year-olds': Pakistani cleric's child bride 'joke' sparks outrage
Article Text:
Mufti Tariq Masood (Source: Wikimedia Commons)

Education and women's autonomy

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Pakistani Islamic preacher Mufti Tariq Masood, who commands a large following across social media platforms, has faced criticism over a series of sermons and remarks defending child marriage.In a report published by Daily Mirror Sri Lanka, the influential Deobandi cleric's comments have been reported in detail.One of the remarks highlighted in the report came from a viral video in which Masood joked that if someone could not find a 16-year-old bride, he could provide “two eight-year-olds” or “four four-year-olds”. The comment drew criticism from people who said it trivialised child marriage and normalised the sexualisation of minors.The Daily Mirror said the backlash was dismissed by supporters as a misunderstanding, with the remark defended as a joke taken out of context.The newspaper also pointed to Masood's repeated opposition to statutory minimum marriage-age laws. According to the report, he has argued that Islamic jurisprudence does not prescribe a universal minimum age of 18 and that parents or guardians should retain discretion over when a girl marries.A recurring theme in his sermons, the newspaper said, is the emphasis on physical development and perceived maturity rather than chronological age when determining whether a girl is ready for marriage. The preacher had made remarks discussing the physical suitability of girls aged nine and ten in the context of marital relations. Pakistan as a country has been grappling with child sexual abuse, forced marriages and gender equality and positioning such leaders as popular figures raises extreme concerns.The Daily Mirror also highlighted Masood's remarks on women's education, saying that some of his statements appear to place a husband's authority above a young wife's decision to continue her studies.It further cited comments about women marrying late, including references to them becoming “aunties”, and discussions of the benefits husbands derive from marriage.Masood has also been criticised for presenting early marriage as a way to manage men's sexual desiresMasood's sermons have reportedly become difficult to access after copyright complaints and takedown requests. Critics have alleged that this limits public scrutiny of his statements, while his supporters maintain that some remarks are circulated without their original context.Masood has built a substantial following on YouTube, Facebook and other social media platforms through a preaching style that combines religious instruction with informal language and humour. His reach extends beyond traditional religious institutions, particularly among younger and urban audiences.
Article Summary: Pakistani Islamic preacher Mufti Tariq Masood has faced criticism over a series of sermons and remarks defending child marriage. In a report published by Daily Mirror Sri Lanka, the influential Deobandi cleric's comments have been reported in detail.

Article Title: Pakistan militant attack kills 10 policemen in KPK's Kohat, gunbattle still under way
Article Text:
No militant organisation has claimed responsibility for the attack so far. (FIle photo)

At least 10 police personnel, including two senior officers, were killed in a militant attack in Pakistan's northwestern Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province on Wednesday, officials told news agency AP.The attack occurred in Kohat district, where militants targeted vehicles carrying police officers, leading to an exchange of gunfire between the attackers and security forces, local police official Faisal Khan said.Khan confirmed that two senior police officers were among those killed. He added that the gunbattle was still underway, but did not share further details.No militant organisation has claimed responsibility for the attack so far. However, suspicion is likely to centre on the Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), also known as the Pakistani Taliban, which has intensified its attacks on security forces in the region in recent months.Pakistan has witnessed a rise in militant violence over the past few years, with much of it attributed to the TTP. The group is separate from the Afghan Taliban but shares close ties with it. The Afghan Taliban returned to power in Afghanistan in 2021.Islamabad has repeatedly accused Afghanistan's Taliban-led government of providing shelter to TTP fighters operating against Pakistan. Kabul has denied the allegations.
Article Summary: At least 10 police personnel, including two senior officers, were killed in a militant attack in Pakistan's northwestern Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province. The attack occurred in Kohat district, where militants targeted vehicles carrying police officers, leading to an exchange of gunfire. No militant organisation has claimed responsibility for the attack so far.

Article Title: Pakistan court frames charges against 8, including grandson of deputy PM Ishaq Dar, in gang rape case
Article Text:
Pakistan deput​y PM Ishaq Dar (File photo)​​

A Pakistani court on Wednesday framed charges against eight suspects, including the grandson of deputy Prime Minister Ishaq Dar, in connection with the gang rape of two foreign women , an official said.All eight accused, including Muhammad Raza Dar, Ishaq Dar's grandson, pleaded not guilty, the official added.“Lahore court judge Rafaqat Ali Gondal framed charges against the suspects, who pleaded not guilty. He directed the prosecution to present its witnesses on December 9 so that the formal trial proceedings could begin,” the official said.Earlier, police in Pakistan's Punjab province had cleared Raza Dar and his four accomplices of charges in the case, instead charging three other employees of Ishaq Dar's grandson of raping the women.The victims were identified as Stephanie Adnana Mau-Arun of the Netherlands and Astrid Robinson Baracho of Venezuela. They were allegedly kidnapped and raped by Raza Dar and his four friends after arriving in Lahore on a business trip in June. Medical examinations confirmed that the women had been raped. They returned to their respective countries after recording their statements.According to the police report, the women met Raza Dar in Singapore in 2025 and invited him to invest in their cryptocurrency business.After receiving returns on his initial investment, he invested more than $500,000. However, the women allegedly failed to provide further returns or repay the amount.In June, Raza Dar invited the women to Pakistan on the pretext of arranging a meeting with another investor. They initially stayed at a hotel in Islamabad and travelled to the hill station of Murree voluntarily.The women were later taken to a house in Lahore's Defence Housing Authority, where they were allegedly held captive and pressured to repay the money. They were forced to transfer $19,500, as per the police report.Armed men guarded the women and threatened them with a knife, a gun and a broken piece of mirror. They also threatened to kill them and sell their body parts if they failed to meet the demands.The women eventually managed to escape after the vehicle in which their alleged captors were taking them to Lahore airport met with an accident.
Article Summary: Pakistani court frames charges against eight suspects in gang rape of two foreign women. All eight accused, including Muhammad Raza Dar, Ishaq Dar's grandson, pleaded not guilty. The victims were identified as Stephanie Adnana Mau-Arun of the Netherlands and Astrid Robinson Baracho of Venezuela.

Article Title: Former Pakistan PM Imran Khan taken to hospital for eye check-up, treatment; shifted back to Adiala Jail
Article Text:
Imran Khan's health sparks concern

Qureshi also hospitalised

Former Pakistan prime minister Imran Khan was taken to hospital for an eye check-up and treatment before being shifted back to prison, news agency Reuters reported on Wednesday, citing officials.Khan, who is lodged in Adiala Jail in Rawalpindi, was taken to the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (PIMS), where he also received treatment for blood pressure-related issues, one of the officials said."He had some blood pressure issues ... and was given required treatment last night. He has been shifted back to his prison cell," the person said.The 74-year-old cricketer-turned-politician has been in prison for more than three years after losing power in a no-confidence vote in 2022. He has faced multiple corruption charges, which he denies, alleging that they are politically motivated. The Shehbaz Sharif government has rejected his claims.All but one of Khan's convictions have been suspended or overturned, with appeals pending.His lawyers have repeatedly raised concerns over his health in prison, claiming that his condition has deteriorated and that he has lost significant vision in his right eye.Wednesday's hospital visit is the first known instance of Khan being taken for treatment and subsequently returned to jail since August, when an earlier hospital visit was cut short.Meanwhile, a Pakistani court has directed jail authorities to allow Khan's legal team to meet him and his wife, his party said.Khan's hospital visit comes a day after his close aide and Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) deputy chairman, Shah Mahmood Qureshi, was taken to a hospital in Lahore after collapsing inside his barrack at Kot Lakhpat Jail.According to a prison official, Qureshi suffered a dizzy spell while walking inside his barrack on Monday, injuring his knee and arm in the fall.The 70-year-old former foreign minister was subsequently shifted to the Punjab Institute of Cardiology for treatment and remains hospitalised.Khan, who led Pakistan to its maiden ODI World Cup title in 1992, has been behind bars for more than three years. Concerns over his health and prison conditions have repeatedly been raised by his family, party members and supporters, including former international cricket colleagues.
Article Summary: Imran Khan was taken to hospital for an eye check-up and treatment before being shifted back to prison. The 74-year-old cricketer-turned-politician has been in prison for more than three years. He has faced multiple corruption charges, which he denies, alleging they are politically motivated.

Article Title: Imran Khan aide, ex-Pakistan foreign minister Shah Mahmood Qureshi collapses in jail; hospitalised
Article Text:
(With PTI inputs)

Pakistan's former foreign minister and Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf vice-chairman Shah Mahmood Qureshi was admitted to a hospital after collapsing in his barrack at a jail in Lahore, a prison official said on Tuesday.According to the official, Qureshi suffered a dizzy spell while walking inside his barrack at Kot Lakhpat Jail on Monday, injuring his knee and arm in the fall.The 70-year-old leader was subsequently shifted to the Punjab Institute of Cardiology for treatment, the official added.Qureshi has been in jail since August 2023 in multiple cases linked to the May 9, 2023, riots, when Tehreek-i-Insaf supporters went on a rampage following the arrest of party chairman and former Prime Minister Imran Khan.Qureshi's counsel, Rana Mudassar Umar, confirmed that the veteran politician was taken to hospital after fainting and suffering a fall.Umar added that the PTI leader would remain under observation for 24 hours, after which doctors would decide whether he should continue treatment at the hospital or be shifted back to jail.Meanwhile, Qureshi's daughter alleged that her father had been jailed on "trumped-up" charges and accused the federal government of keeping him behind bars with "malafide" intent."Three and a half years ago, a hale and hearty lion heart was sent to jail on trumped-up charges. He not only fought the cypher case with resolve and courage but refused to sacrifice his principles at the altar of self-interest," Mehr Bano said."My father has been acquitted multiple times but remains behind bars due to the government's malafide. Over 90 bail hearings have gone by, but the record has yet to be produced. A man whose innocence has been proven again and again is being held... It is high time the judge establishes his authority and grants him bail," she demanded.Bano also highlighted her father's more than four decades of public service in Pakistan."He has served twice as Pakistan's foreign minister, and as parliamentary leader and vice-chairman of Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf, he has fulfilled important responsibilities and protected Pakistan's interests. He has fought for the supremacy of the Constitution and democracy. He deserves justice and freedom," she stated.
Article Summary: Pakistan's former foreign minister Shah Mahmood Qureshi was admitted to a hospital after collapsing in his barrack at a jail in Lahore. The 70-year-old has been in jail since August 2023 in multiple cases linked to the May 9, 2023, riots. His daughter has accused the federal government of keeping him behind bars with "malafide" intent.

Article Title: Bangladesh garment owners threaten to quit wage talks, shut factories indefinitely
Article Text:
File photo: Garment workers exchange words with security forces outside a factory as they protest demanding higher wages in Mirpur, Dhaka, Bangladesh

Wage talks face fresh uncertainty

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Garment manufacturers in Bangladesh have threatened to withdraw from minimum wage negotiations and shut factories indefinitely if workers continue vandalising industrial units during protests.The Bangladesh Garment Manufacturers and Exporters Association (BGMEA) and Bangladesh Knitwear Manufacturers and Exporters Association (BKMEA) said on Saturday that they were reconsidering their participation in the wage talks, citing a lack of assurances over factory security."If the situation persists, we must reconsider," BGMEA president Mahmud Hasan Khan said at a news briefing in Dhaka, referring to the next round of negotiations scheduled for Monday.Khan also said factories unable to operate because of the unrest would remain closed indefinitely under Bangladesh's labour law. Section 13(1) of the Bangladesh Labour Act allows employers to suspend operations under a "no work, no pay" provision.The warning comes after weeks of protests over wages and working conditions, with demonstrations turning violent in several garment manufacturing centres. Workers have blocked roads, while clashes this month have involved damage to property and the torching of police vehicles.At least 147 factories remained closed on Saturday across Savar, Ashulia and Gazipur, the country's major garment manufacturing hubs. More than 4,500 factories are registered with industry trade bodies.The Minimum Wage Board, formed on November 1, is due to meet on Monday to discuss a revised pay structure for garment workers. The current minimum monthly wage stands at Tk12,500 (approx INR 9479), fixed in December 2023.Workers' representatives have proposed raising the minimum to Tk32,000 (approx INR 24267), more than double the existing rate, according to local media reports. The demand has also been reported at Tk30,000 (approx INR 22751) in other accounts.The workers' proposal includes Tk19,200 (approx INR 14560) in basic pay, Tk9,600 (approx INR 7280) in house rent and Tk3,200 (approx INR 2426) in allowances covering medical expenses, transport, food and other costs. It also proposes four wage grades, with monthly salaries ranging from Tk32,000 (approx INR 24267) to Tk48,000 (approx INR 36401).Factory owners have yet to submit their formal proposal. They were given four days after the November 9 meeting to prepare their recommendations, which are expected to be discussed at Monday's session. Local media reports said employers could submit their proposal while staying away from the meeting.Workers say their wages have failed to keep pace with the rising cost of food, housing, transport and healthcare. Inflation in Bangladesh is running at around 8%, further eroding their purchasing power.The minimum wage has risen consistently in Bangladesh but despite these increases, Bangladesh's garment workers remain among the lower-paid in the region.The threat of an indefinite shutdown has already materialised at several units. Seven factories in Savar and Ashulia have been closed under Section 13(1), according to local media reports.The disruption has prompted concern over the impact on an industry that employs more than four million people and accounts for roughly 80% of Bangladesh's export earnings.The timing is particularly sensitive, with factories entering the run-up to Christmas, traditionally one of the busiest periods for garment exports.For an industry already facing pressure over production costs, the combination of unresolved wage demands, factory shutdowns and the risk of losing buyer confidence could make the coming weeks critical.
Article Summary: Bangladesh Garment Manufacturers and Exporters Association (BGMEA) says it is reconsidering participation in wage talks. The warning comes after weeks of protests over wages and working conditions. At least 147 factories remained closed on Saturday across Savar, Ashulia and Gazipur, the country's major garment manufacturing hubs.
